name: Hebrews
subtitle: An Argument Made of Scripture
howToRead: Hebrews never says "as it is written." It simply lets God speak the older words again, now to the Son. Chapter 1 is itself a catena — a chain of seven citations strung against the angels. Each chip below a passage points back to its source; click it to read the precursor, its kind (quotation, allusion, echo, or figural), and why it is heard here. Where the author quotes the Greek Bible against the Hebrew, the chip is marked contested.

pericopes.text: God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds. His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, who, when he had by himself purified us of our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high; having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they have.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty’ (v. 3) is a low-volume echo of Ps 110:1, planted before the catena begins and paid off as its explicit climax at 1:13. Hays' recurrence test: the same source surfaces twice, so even the faint first instance earns credence.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘When he had by himself purified us of our sins’ (v. 3) quotes nothing, yet figurally invokes the Day of Atonement cult that chapters 9–10 will expound — the book's central typology. No verbal volume; high figural coherence (Hays, Reading Backwards).

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, and a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, and an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26)
echoes.note: The marquee echo of the chapter. ‘Radiance of his glory… the very image of his substance’ (v. 3) reproduces the rare term apaugasma and the eikōn/glory pairing of Wis 7:25–26 — high verbal volume against a Second Temple text most scholars (Hays, Attridge, Beale & Carson) name as the direct source. Hebrews transfers what Wisdom says of personified Sophia to the Son. Confidence kept high despite low text-field availability, since bible-api serves only the Protestant canon.

echoes.text: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep, when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong, when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth; then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
echoes.note: ‘Through whom also he made the worlds’ (v. 2) draws on the Wisdom-as-agent-of-creation tradition that runs from Prov 8:22–31 into Wisdom and Sirach. Thematic coherence (Wisdom christology) more than verbal volume; the LXX of Prov 8:22 (‘the Lord created me’) fed the patristic debates this verse anticipates.

echoes.text: Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession.
echoes.note: ‘Whom he appointed heir of all things’ (v. 2) sounds the inheritance grant of Ps 2:8 — the same psalm quoted outright at 1:5. Recurrence (Hays): Ps 2 is demonstrably available and re-used, so the inheritance language is heard as its anticipatory echo.

echoes.text: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.
echoes.note: ‘Heir of all things’ and the universal, unending dominion granted the one ‘like a son of man’ (Dan 7:14) share thematic coherence with the Son's inheritance and session. Faint, contested — no verbal volume — but a stock messianic substrate scholars note behind the exaltation language.

echoes.text: Yahweh, your Redeemer, and he who formed you from the womb says: ‘I am Yahweh, who makes all things; who alone stretches out the heavens; who spreads out the earth by myself;’
echoes.note: ‘Upholding all things by the word of his power’ (v. 3) ascribes to the Son the sole-creator role Isa 44:24 reserves to YHWH — a faint conceptual echo that prepares the bolder Ps 102 transfer at 1:10–12. Low volume; coherence with the creation theme of the prologue.

echoes.text: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh,
echoes.note: ‘Having become so much better than the angels’ (v. 4) faintly recalls the incomparability formula of Ps 89:6, which sets YHWH above the ‘sons of the heavenly beings.’ A dashed echo seeding the angel-comparison the catena exists to make; Ps 89 recurs at 1:6 (‘firstborn’).

pericopes.text: For to which of the angels did he say at any time, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father?’ and again, ‘I will be to him a Father, and he will be to me a Son?’

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’
echoes.note: The royal-enthronement decree, applied to the Son. Verbatim (high volume) and recurrent — Ps 2 returns at Heb 5:5. The first link in the chain.

echoes.text: I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: Nathan's dynastic oracle to David, read messianically and welded to Ps 2:7 by shared father/son language — a classic gezerah shavah (linking two texts by a common phrase). The author silently drops the clause about iniquity.

echoes.text: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh, (Psalm 89:6; vv. 26–27: ‘He will call to me, “You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.” I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.’)
echoes.note: Ps 89:26–27 reworks the Nathan oracle into ‘You are my Father… I will appoint him my firstborn,’ the same father/firstborn nexus Hebrews exploits across 1:5–6. The verbatim text-field shows Ps 89:6 (what bible-api returns for psalm+89:6); the relevant 26–27 wording is quoted inline. Medium volume, strong thematic coherence linking this verse to 1:6's prōtotokos.

echoes.text: He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
echoes.note: The clause immediately preceding the quoted 7:14 promises an everlasting throne — the dynastic-permanence note Hebrews develops into the eternal Son (cf. ‘your throne… forever’ at 1:8). A contiguous echo riding on the formal citation.

echoes.text: I will be his father, and he will be my son. I will not take my loving kindness away from him, as I took it from him that was before you;
echoes.note: The Chronicler's parallel of the Nathan oracle drops the conditional ‘if he commits iniquity,’ giving the unconditioned father/son form Hebrews actually uses. A faint witness that the author's tradition already read the oracle as Hebrews does; low independent volume.

pericopes.text: When he again brings in the firstborn into the world he says, ‘Let all the angels of God worship him.’

echoes.text: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
echoes.note: A textual fork. The Hebrew of Deut 32:43 (‘Rejoice, you nations, with his people…’) has no such line; the clause exists only in the Septuagint the author read. Hays' first test — availability — in action: the Scripture available to him was the Greek Bible, and that is the text he quotes.
echoes.lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

echoes.text: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
echoes.note: ‘The firstborn’ (prōtotokos) carries the Davidic-king title of Ps 89:27 — a verbal allusion, not a formal citation, transferring the king's rank to the Son.

echoes.text: Let all them be shamed who serve engraved images, who boast in their idols. Worship him, all you gods!
echoes.note: The LXX of Ps 97:7 renders the Hebrew ‘all you gods (elohim)’ as ‘all his angels,’ giving the very clause Hebrews cites — hence many (Beale & Carson, NA28 margin) read Ps 97:7 LXX, not Deut 32:43, as the primary source. The WEB (Hebrew) shown here lacks the angelic wording; the divergence is the whole contest. A theophany-of-judgment psalm bent to the enthronement of the firstborn.
echoes.lxxText: Let all that worship graven images be ashamed, who boast of their idols; worship him, all ye his angels.

echoes.text: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
echoes.note: The Masoretic Hebrew of Deut 32:43 (shown here) shows what the Greek expanded: no command to worship and no angels. Included to mark the Hebrew-vs-LXX gap figurally — the Song of Moses' eschatological vindication is the frame into which the Greek tradition inserted the angelic homage Hebrews needs. Low volume; contested.
echoes.lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

pericopes.text: Of the angels he says, ‘Who makes his angels winds, and his servants a flame of fire.’

echoes.text: He makes his messengers winds; his servants flames of fire.
echoes.note: A creation psalm. The Hebrew (here, WEB) reads ‘makes winds his messengers’; Hebrews follows the Greek word order — ‘makes his angels winds’ — bending the line toward angelology. The same reversible ambiguity the argument needs: angels are mutable servants, the Son is enthroned.
echoes.lxxText: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire.

echoes.text: lightning and hail, snow and clouds; stormy wind, fulfilling his word;
echoes.note: The picture of wind and fire as God's compliant agents (‘stormy wind, fulfilling his word’) shares the mutable-creature theme Hebrews presses against the angels. A faint thematic echo, no verbal volume — listed for the maximal inventory.

pericopes.text: But of the Son he says, ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your Kingdom. You have loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.’

echoes.text: Your throne, God, is forever and ever. A scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness, and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.
echoes.note: A royal wedding psalm in which the king is addressed as ‘God.’ Hebrews reads the vocative christologically — the figural payload (the Son addressed as God) rides on a high-volume, verbatim quotation.

echoes.text: You are the most excellent of the sons of men. Grace has anointed your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.
echoes.note: The same psalm opens by setting the king ‘above the sons of men,’ matching ‘above your fellows’ (v. 9). A contiguous echo from the immediate context of the citation, reinforcing the Son's surpassing rank (recurrence within one source).

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: ‘Has anointed you with the oil of gladness’ (v. 9) draws on the messianic-anointing register that Isa 61:1 made canonical for the title ‘Christ/anointed.’ Faint, no verbal volume — thematic coherence with the Son's anointing above his fellows.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

echoes.text: The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me, ‘One who rules over men righteously, who rules in the fear of God,
echoes.note: ‘You have loved righteousness’ (v. 9) sits within the ‘last words of David,’ where the ideal ruler is defined by righteous rule. A low-volume conceptual echo of the just-king ideal Hebrews applies to the Son.

pericopes.text: And, ‘You, Lord, in the beginning, laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you continue. They all will grow old like a garment does. You will roll them up like a mantle, and they will be changed; but you are the same. Your years will not fail.’

echoes.text: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.
echoes.note: The boldest move in the catena: a psalm addressed to YHWH the creator is applied to the Son. Thematic coherence with the prologue — ‘through whom he made the worlds’ (1:2) — is what licenses the transfer.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens will vanish away like smoke, and the earth will wear out like a garment; and its inhabitants will die in the same way: but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will not be abolished.
echoes.note: ‘They all will grow old like a garment’ (v. 11) shares the exact heavens-wear-out-like-a-garment versus God-endures contrast of Isa 51:6 — the same cosmic-impermanence topos that stands behind the Ps 102 citation. Medium volume on the ‘garment’ simile; strong thematic coherence.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: ‘You will roll them up like a mantle’ (v. 12) echoes the apocalyptic ‘sky rolled up like a scroll’ of Isa 34:4 (cf. Rev 6:14). The rolling-up image reinforces the dissolution of the heavens against the Son's permanence; an allusion clustering with the Ps 102 quotation.

echoes.text: But you, Yahweh, will remain forever; your renown endures to all generations.
echoes.note: Within the same psalm, v. 12 already voices the ‘but you remain’ permanence that vv. 25–27 cosmologize. ‘But you are the same. Your years will not fail’ (v. 12 of Hebrews) sounds this nearer verse too — recurrence inside the cited source.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning, laid the foundation of the earth’ (v. 10) reaches back to the opening of creation itself (Gen 1:1), now spoken to the Son. Faint verbal contact on ‘in the beginning… heavens and earth’; figural coherence with the Son as agent of creation.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: ‘But you are the same’ (v. 12) — the divine immutability — figurally invokes the self-identical ‘I AM’ of Exod 3:14, the name of the unchanging God now predicated of the Son. No verbal volume; a contested figural reading scholars note behind Hebrews' immutability claims (cf. 13:8).

pericopes.text: But which of the angels has he told at any time, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet?’

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: The session-at-the-right-hand oracle, the most-cited verse in the New Testament. It pays off the quiet echo of v. 3 and brackets the chapter — Hays' recurrence and satisfaction tests both met.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: ‘Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’ shares the ‘all things under his feet’ subjection imagery of Ps 8:6 — the very psalm Hebrews quotes next at 2:6–8. Recurrence (Hays): the two enthronement texts are linked by the shared ‘feet’ motif (gezerah shavah), and Ps 8 is demonstrably available across the seam of chapters 1–2.

pericopes.text: Aren't they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh, you angels of his, who are mighty in strength, who fulfill his word, obeying the voice of his word. Praise Yahweh, all you armies of his, you servants of his, who do his pleasure.
echoes.note: Angels as ‘serving spirits’ who do God's bidding echoes the obedient heavenly host of Ps 103:20–21 — conceptual rather than verbatim (a dashed allusion). It closes the angel/Son contrast the catena was built to make.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.
echoes.note: ‘Sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation’ recalls the protective, ministering commission of angels in Ps 91:11. A faint thematic echo of the angels-serve-the-faithful motif; no verbal volume, included for the maximal inventory.

pericopes.text: Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that were heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense; how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation—which at the first having been spoken through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard; God also testifying with them, both by signs and wonders, by various works of power, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will?

echoes.text: Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran. He came from the ten thousands of holy ones. At his right hand was a fiery law for them.
echoes.note: ‘The word spoken through angels’ (v. 2) invokes the tradition that the Law was mediated at Sinai by angels — read out of the Greek of Deut 33:2 and assumed in Acts 7:53 and Gal 3:19. The lesser, angel-given word frames the argument that the Son's word is greater.

pericopes.text: For he didn't subject the world to come, of which we speak, to angels. But one has somewhere testified, saying, ‘What is man, that you think of him? Or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels. You crowned him with glory and honor. You have put all things in subjection under his feet.’ For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But now we don't see all things subjected to him, yet. But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone.

echoes.text: what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? For you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor. You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: A psalm on humanity's place in creation. Hebrews hears ‘son of man’ christologically and presses ‘a little lower than the angels’ against the temporary humiliation of Jesus — the ‘not yet’ of v. 8 is the whole argument. High volume; the figural turn rides on the quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: Beale & Carson note that Hebrews reads Ps 8's ‘all things under his feet’ through Ps 110:1's ‘enemies… your footstool’ — the same subjection-of-all language welded the two psalms together (gezerah shavah). Recurrence is high: Ps 110:1 brackets ch. 1 (1:3, 1:13) and returns at 10:12–13, so its subjection motif is audible behind the ‘nothing… not subject to him’ of v. 8.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Hays' thematic-coherence test: the ‘son of man’ who is given ‘dominion… glory… and a kingdom’ over ‘all’ coheres with Hebrews' enthroned-and-crowned Son, leading many to hear Dan 7's heavenly ‘son of man’ resonating beneath the Ps 8 ‘son of man’ — the human title carrying eschatological dominion. Verbal volume is low (the shared phrase ‘son of man,’ huios anthrōpou, is generic in the LXX), so the link is contested.
echoes.altSource: Psalm 8:4 (the only formally cited ‘son of man’)

echoes.text: When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the children of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: Faint and contested. ‘He didn't subject the world to come… to angels’ (v. 5) is heard by some against the Second Temple reading of Deut 32:8 — where the LXX/Qumran witnesses read ‘according to the number of the angels [sons of God],’ implying the present-age nations were apportioned to angelic powers while the ‘world to come’ is reserved for the Son. The WEB above follows the Masoretic ‘children of Israel’; the divergence is exactly the LXX-vs-Hebrew fork on which the echo depends, so volume is low.

pericopes.text: For it became him, for whom are all things, and through whom are all things, in bringing many children to glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one, for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, ‘I will declare your name to my brothers. Among of the congregation I will sing your praise.’ Again, ‘I will put my trust in him.’ Again, ‘Behold, here I am with the children whom God has given me.’

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: From the great psalm of the righteous sufferer (Ps 22, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me’). The vindicated one calls the redeemed ‘brothers’ — the citation grounds the solidarity Hebrews needs between the Son and the ‘many children.’

echoes.text: I will wait for Yahweh, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him.
echoes.note: ‘I will put my trust in him’ follows the Greek of Isa 8:17; the same clause appears at 2 Sam 22:3 and Isa 12:2 LXX, so the exact source is debated. Volume is low (one clause), but its pairing with the next line from the same Isaiah passage tips the identification toward Isa 8.

echoes.text: Behold, I and the children whom Yahweh has given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from Yahweh of Armies, who dwells in Mount Zion.
echoes.note: Quoted immediately after 8:17 from the same breath of Isaiah. The prophet's ‘children’ become the Son's ‘children’ — Isaiah's household read as a figure of the redeemed gathered around Christ.

echoes.text: Behold, God is my salvation. I will trust, and will not be afraid; for Yah, Yahweh, is my strength and song; and he has become my salvation.”
echoes.note: Listed as the competing source for ‘I will put my trust in him’: Isa 12:2 LXX reads pepoithōs esomai ep' autō, verbally even closer than Isa 8:17. Beale & Carson treat it as the likeliest single donor, so it is heard here as a low-volume alternate behind the same clause. Contested precisely because Hebrews seems to have conflated the Isaianic ‘trust’ texts.
echoes.altSource: Isaiah 8:17 (printed above as the primary identification)

echoes.text:
Of you comes my praise in the great assembly.
I will pay my vows before those who fear him.
echoes.note: A faint recurrence echo: having quoted Ps 22:22, the author's ‘in the congregation I will sing your praise’ keeps sounding the same psalm's assembly-of-praise language (Ps 22:25, ‘praise in the great assembly’). Low verbal volume beyond the shared ‘assembly/praise,’ but Hays' recurrence test favors hearing the wider psalm once it has been opened.

echoes.text: But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is of disservice to us, and is contrary to our works, and upbraids us with sins against the law... But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will touch them. (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12; 3:1)
echoes.note: Several scholars (noted in Beale & Carson) hear the Wisdom-of-Solomon portrait of the righteous sufferer, perfected and numbered among God's ‘sons,’ behind Heb 2:10's ‘author of their salvation perfect through sufferings’ bringing ‘many sons to glory.’ Thematic coherence is strong; verbal volume is low and the source is deuterocanonical, hence low confidence.

echoes.text: He shall sprinkle of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it, and make it holy from the uncleanness of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: ‘He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified’ (v. 11) anticipates the sanctifying, sin-cleansing high-priestly work that chs. 9–10 ground in the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). No verbal volume — a faint forward-pointing figure of the cult the letter will expound, consistent with the seeding pattern Hays calls satisfaction.

pericopes.text: Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. For most certainly, he doesn't give help to angels, but he gives help to the offspring of Abraham. Therefore he was obligated in all things to be made like his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘To make atonement for the sins of the people’ (v. 17) reintroduces the Day of Atonement figure first sounded at 1:3 and expounded in chs 9–10. No quotation — the high-priestly, sacrificial pattern itself is the borrowing (figural). The recurrence is the point: the motif is being seeded before the argument arrives.

echoes.text: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham my friend, You whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant, I have chosen you and have not cast you away.’
echoes.note: ‘He gives help to the offspring of Abraham’ (v. 16) echoes Isa 41:8–9, where God ‘takes hold of’ (epilambanomai, the very verb Hebrews uses) the chosen ‘offspring of Abraham’ his servant. The shared rare verb plus the ‘seed of Abraham’ phrase gives real verbal volume; thematic coherence (election, help, servant) is strong, so the allusion is widely heard (Beale & Carson).

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.
echoes.note: ‘Through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil’ (v. 14) is read by many as the protoevangelium fulfilled: the woman's offspring crushing the serpent's head, the serpent being identified with the devil in Second Temple and NT tradition. No verbal volume — a figural/typological link resting on thematic coherence (the seed defeats the death-dealing adversary).

echoes.text: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and those who are of his portion make trial thereof. (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24)
echoes.note: Wisdom 2:24 is the standard Second Temple text identifying the devil with the bringer of death, exactly the equation Heb 2:14 makes (‘him who had the power of death, that is, the devil’). Beale & Carson cite it for the conceptual background; verbal volume is nil and the source deuterocanonical, hence low confidence and an echo at the level of shared idea.

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? ‘Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.’
echoes.note: ‘Deliver all of them who through fear of death were… subject to bondage’ (vv. 14–15) faintly sounds Hosea's promise to ransom from ‘the power of death/Sheol.’ The taunt over death's power coheres with Hebrews' deliverance theme (and with 1 Cor 15:55, which quotes it), but verbal volume here is low and the link is contested.

pericopes.text: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Jesus; who was faithful to him who appointed him, as also was Moses in all his house. For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, because he who built the house has more honor than the house. For every house is built by someone; but he who built all things is God. Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were afterward to be spoken, but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house; whose house we are, if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end.

echoes.text: My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house.
echoes.note: God's own commendation of Moses — ‘faithful in all my house’ — is woven in twice (vv. 2, 5) and then turned on its pivot: Moses faithful as a servant in the house, Christ faithful as a Son over it. The whole Moses/Christ comparison hangs on this one verse.

echoes.text: He said, “Hear now my words. If there is a prophet among you, I Yahweh will make myself known to him in a vision. I will speak with him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house. With him I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: The wider Numbers 12 oracle, not just v. 7, shapes the comparison: Moses is the unrivaled prophet who sees God's form and is ‘faithful in all my house,’ and Hebrews silently grants him that supreme rank in order to place Christ higher still. Hays' criterion of thematic coherence: the ‘servant… in the house’ vs. ‘Son… over the house’ antithesis presupposes the whole oracle, where Moses' unique status is precisely the point being surpassed.

echoes.text: He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The wordplay on ‘house’ (the one who builds it has more honor, vv. 3–4) draws on Nathan's oracle, where ‘house’ slides between temple and dynasty and the Davidic son who ‘builds a house’ is also called God's ‘son.’ Hebrews has already quoted 2 Sam 7:14 at 1:5 (recurrence), and here the building-the-house / Son-over-the-house logic coheres with the same Davidic son-and-house complex.

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Yahweh of Armies says, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.”’
echoes.note: The fusion of house-builder, royal Son, and priest in 3:1–6 (the ‘High Priest’ who ‘built the house’ and rules ‘as a Son over his house’) coheres with Zechariah's Branch, who alone among the prophets both builds the temple and is ‘a priest on his throne.’ Low verbal volume and contested, but the king-builds-temple-and-is-priest pattern is the conceptual world Hebrews assumes.

echoes.text: He shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. I will not take my loving kindness away from him, as I took it from him that was before you; but I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever. His throne shall be established forever.”
echoes.note: The Chronicler's recension of Nathan's oracle sharpens the ‘house’ motif — ‘I will settle him in my house’ — and so reinforces the same Davidic son-and-house pattern behind 3:6 (‘a Son over his house; whose house we are’). A faint, redundant echo flagged for completeness; verbal volume is low and it largely overlaps 2 Sam 7.

pericopes.text: Therefore, even as the Holy Spirit says, ‘Today if you will hear his voice, don't harden your hearts, as in the rebellion, like as in the day of the trial in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me by proving me, and saw my deeds for forty years. Therefore I was displeased with that generation, and said, “They always err in their heart, but they didn't know my ways;” as I swore in my wrath, “They will not enter into my rest.”’

echoes.text: for he is our God. We are the people of his pasture, and the sheep in his care. Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my work. Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, ‘It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.’ Therefore I swore in my wrath, ‘They won't enter into my rest.’
echoes.note: The text the next chapter and a half expounds. Attributed not to David but to ‘the Holy Spirit’ speaking ‘today’ — Hebrews treats the psalm as a live word addressed to its own hearers. The wilderness generation's forfeited ‘rest’ becomes the standing warning.

echoes.text: because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.
echoes.note: Psalm 95 is itself a poetic compression of this Numbers 14 verdict, and Hebrews mines it directly: ‘tested me… saw my deeds’ (v. 9) answers ‘seen my glory and my signs… tempted me,’ while the sworn exclusion ‘they shall not see the land’ underlies ‘they will not enter into my rest.’ Hays' recurrence and thematic coherence: the wilderness-rebellion narrative is the substrate the homily presupposes and re-mines in 3:16–18.

echoes.text: Tell them, ‘As I live, says Yahweh, surely as you have spoken in my ears, so will I do to you. Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness; and all who were counted of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me, surely you shall not come into the land, concerning which I swore that I would make you dwell therein, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun. But your little ones, that you said should be captured or killed, them I will bring in, and they shall know the land which you have rejected. But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness. After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years, and you will know my alienation.’ I, Yahweh, have spoken. I will surely do this to all this evil congregation, who are gathered together against me. In this wilderness they shall be consumed, and there they shall die.”
echoes.note: God's sworn sentence on the wilderness generation supplies both the divine oath (‘I swore… they will not enter,’ v. 11) and the ‘forty years’ (v. 9) that Hebrews will press in 3:17 (‘whose bodies fell in the wilderness’). High thematic coherence and recurrence across the pericope; the oath-formula ‘surely you shall not come into the land’ is the precursor of ‘they will not enter into my rest.’

echoes.text: He called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because the children of Israel quarreled, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us, or not?”
echoes.note: ‘The rebellion… the day of the trial’ (vv. 8–9) renders the LXX of Ps 95, which itself flattens the place-names Meribah/Massah (‘quarreling/testing’) into common nouns; behind them stands Exodus 17:7, the founding episode where Israel ‘tested Yahweh.’ LXX-vs-Hebrew divergence: where the Hebrew psalm names the places, the Greek the author quotes generalizes them to ‘rebellion’ and ‘testing,’ loosening the link to Exod 17 while preserving the motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh heard the voice of your words, and was angry, and swore, saying, “Surely not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land, which I swore to give to your fathers,
echoes.note: Moses' own retelling of the verdict in Deuteronomy doubles the oath behind ‘as I swore in my wrath, they will not enter into my rest’ (v. 11): God ‘was angry, and swore… not one of this evil generation shall see the good land.’ The recurrence of the sworn exclusion across Num 14 / Deut 1 strengthens the thematic coherence Hebrews exploits.

echoes.text: and might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation that didn’t make their hearts loyal, whose spirit was not steadfast with God.
echoes.note: Psalm 78, the other great wilderness-rebellion psalm, supplies the ‘stubborn and rebellious generation’ whose ‘heart’ was not right — coherent with ‘they always err in their heart’ (v. 10) and ‘don't harden your hearts.’ Faint and contested (no verbal citation), included as part of the maximal wilderness substrate scholars hear behind the homily.

pericopes.text: Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God; but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’; lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold fast the beginning of our confidence firm to the end: while it is said, ‘Today if you will hear his voice, don't harden your hearts, as in the rebellion.’ For who, when they heard, rebelled? No, didn't all those who came out of Egypt by Moses? With whom was he displeased forty years? Wasn't it with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? To whom did he swear that they wouldn't enter into his rest, but to those who were disobedient? We see that they were not able to enter in because of unbelief.

echoes.text: Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness
echoes.note: The homily keeps re-sounding its own text — re-citing ‘Today…’ at v. 15 and then mining each phrase (‘today,’ ‘harden,’ ‘rest,’ ‘they could not enter’). Recurrence is doing the interpretive work (Hays): the same verses return until the warning lands.

echoes.text: Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness; and all who were counted of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me,
echoes.note: ‘Whose bodies fell in the wilderness’ (v. 17) is a near-verbatim borrowing of Num 14:29 (LXX: ‘your corpses shall fall in this wilderness’) — the highest-volume verbal link in the pericope. Hebrews lifts the very phrase, then makes ‘they were not able to enter in because of unbelief’ (v. 19) the moral. Verbal volume and recurrence both high.

echoes.text: because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.
echoes.note: The sworn exclusion ‘surely they shall not see the land’ stands directly behind ‘to whom did he swear that they wouldn't enter… we see that they were not able to enter in’ (vv. 18–19). The same Numbers 14 oath that Ps 95:11 versifies is now read back through the narrative. Recurrence across 3:7–11 and 3:12–19 ties the homily's argument to the Pentateuchal source.

echoes.text: surely you shall not come into the land, concerning which I swore that I would make you dwell therein, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
echoes.note: The oath ‘you shall not come into the land… concerning which I swore’ is the precise template of ‘to whom did he swear that they wouldn't enter into his rest’ (v. 18), with ‘land’ transposed to ‘rest.’ The named exceptions (Caleb and Joshua) silently underwrite Hebrews' later Joshua/rest argument at 4:8. Thematic coherence high; verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: Remember, and don’t forget, how you provoked Yahweh your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day that you left the land of Egypt, until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against Yahweh.
echoes.note: Moses' summary indictment — Israel ‘rebellious against Yahweh’ from Egypt onward — coheres with ‘who, when they heard, rebelled? … all those who came out of Egypt by Moses’ (v. 16). Faint and contested (no citation), folded in as part of the wider Deuteronomic wilderness-rebellion frame the homily presumes.

echoes.text: These are the waters of Meribah; because the children of Israel strove with Yahweh, and he was sanctified in them.
echoes.note: The Meribah tradition (which Ps 95:8 names) recurs at Num 20, the rebellion that even barred Moses from the land — a faint figural deepening of ‘they were not able to enter in.’ Very low volume and contested; included for maximal coverage of the strife-in-the-wilderness substrate.

pericopes.text: Let us fear therefore, lest perhaps anyone of you should seem to have come short of a promise of entering into his rest. For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn't profit them, because it wasn't mixed with faith by those who heard. For we who have believed do enter into that rest, even as he has said, ‘As I swore in my wrath, they will not enter into my rest’; although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has said this somewhere about the seventh day, ‘God rested on the seventh day from all his works’; and in this place again, ‘They will not enter into my rest.’

echoes.text: Therefore I swore in my wrath, ‘They won't enter into my rest.’
echoes.note: The ‘rest’ clause is lifted out and turned on a hinge: if God still says ‘today,’ the rest must remain open. Recurrence again — the argument advances by re-citing a single phrase.

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
echoes.note: Joined to Ps 95 by the catchword ‘rest’ (gezerah shavah): God's own Sabbath rest at creation defines the ‘rest’ the psalm holds open. Two texts fused by a shared word to make a third meaning.

echoes.text: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished.
echoes.note: ‘Although the works were finished from the foundation of the world’ (v. 3) echoes the completion formula of Gen 2:1, immediately preceding the Sabbath verse the author goes on to quote. Verbal volume is modest (the verb ‘finished/completed,’ synteleō in the LXX), but its tight pairing with the Gen 2:2 quotation (recurrence within one breath) makes the allusion audible: the rest is grounded in a creation already complete.

echoes.text: but in very deed, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with Yahweh's glory; because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.
echoes.note: The oath of exclusion that Ps 95:11 itself recalls originates in Num 14, the Kadesh rebellion: God swears that the unbelieving wilderness generation ‘will not see the land.’ Hebrews quotes the psalm, but the narrative substrate (‘the word they heard didn't profit them, because it wasn't mixed with faith,’ v. 2) is the Numbers episode. Thematic coherence is strong; the link is mediated through the psalm rather than cited directly, hence allusion.

echoes.text: Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness
echoes.note: ‘We have had good news preached to us, even as they also did’ (v. 2) keeps the ‘today’ frame of the homily's governing text alive even before it is re-cited in 4:7. Low verbal volume here, but the recurrence of Ps 95 across chs 3–4 (Hays) licenses hearing its opening summons under the contrast between the two audiences who ‘heard.’

pericopes.text: Seeing therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and they to whom the good news was preached before failed to enter in because of disobedience, he again defines a certain day, today, saying through David so long a time afterward (just as has been said), ‘Today if you will hear his voice, don't harden your hearts.’ For if Joshua had given them rest, he would not have spoken afterward of another day. There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Let us therefore give diligence to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall after the same example of disobedience.

echoes.text: Today, oh that you would hear his voice! Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness
echoes.note: Re-cited a final time and dated: ‘through David so long a time afterward.’ Because the psalm still says ‘today’ centuries after Joshua, the promised rest was never exhausted by entering Canaan — a chronological argument from a single recurring word. The pun underneath: ‘Joshua’ and ‘Jesus’ are one name in Greek, so the rest Joshua could not give, Jesus does.

echoes.text: Yahweh gave them rest all around, according to all that he swore to their fathers. Not a man of all their enemies stood before them. Yahweh delivered all their enemies into their hand.
echoes.note: ‘For if Joshua had given them rest…’ (v. 8) plays directly against the conquest narrative's own claim that Joshua did give Israel ‘rest’ (Josh 21:44). Hebrews concedes the historical rest only to deny it was the final one — high thematic coherence, and the Greek Iēsous makes ‘Joshua’ and ‘Jesus’ the same name, sharpening the typology. Verbal volume rests on the keyword katepausen / katapausis (‘gave rest’/‘rest’).

echoes.text: Now Yahweh your God has given rest to your brothers, as he spoke to them. Therefore now return and go to your tents, to the land of your possession, which Moses the servant of Yahweh gave you beyond the Jordan.
echoes.note: A second statement that ‘Yahweh your God has given rest’ under Joshua, reinforcing the conquest-rest that Heb 4:8 declares incomplete. Lower volume than 21:44 but the same catchword (‘given rest’) and theme; scholars (Beale & Carson) note both as the background to the Joshua argument.

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
echoes.note: ‘He who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his’ (v. 10) re-sounds Gen 2:2 (quoted at 4:4) to define the promised rest as a sharing in God's own Sabbath — the coinage sabbatismos (‘a Sabbath rest,’ v. 9) is built on it. Recurrence within the same pericope cluster (Hays).

echoes.text: for you haven't yet come to the rest and to the inheritance, which Yahweh your God gives you. But when you go over the Jordan, and dwell in the land which Yahweh your God causes you to inherit, and he gives you rest from all your enemies around you, so that you dwell in safety;
echoes.note: Deuteronomy already pairs ‘rest’ (menuchah / katapausis) with ‘inheritance,’ defining the land-entry as the moment Israel reaches ‘the rest.’ Some commentators hear it behind Hebrews' fusion of rest-language with promise/inheritance; the link is faint (no verbal quotation, mediated through the broader rest-tradition), hence a low-confidence allusion.

pericopes.text: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account. Having then a great high priest, who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold tightly to our confession. For we don't have a high priest who can't be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy, and may find grace for help in time of need.

echoes.text: He has made my mouth like a sharp sword. He has hidden me in the shadow of his hand. He has made me a polished shaft. He has kept me close in his quiver.
echoes.note: ‘The word of God… sharper than any two-edged sword’ (v. 12) draws on the prophetic image of speech as a sword — the Servant's mouth ‘like a sharp sword’ in Isa 49:2. Verbal volume is the shared ‘sharp sword’ + ‘word/mouth’ collocation; Hays' criterion of thematic coherence (God's effective utterance) supports it, though Hebrews has no formula and the trope is widespread (cf. Isa 11:4; Eph 6:17; Rev 1:16).

echoes.text: Your all-powerful word leaped from heaven out of the royal throne, A stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land, Bearing as a sharp sword your unfeigned commandment; And standing it filled all things with death; And while it touched the heaven it trode upon the earth.
echoes.note: The closest single parallel: in Wisdom God's hypostatized ‘all-powerful word’ (logos) is a warrior ‘bearing as a sharp sword’ God's commandment and is ‘living/active’ in execution. Hebrews shares the personification of the logos as a living, sword-bearing agent — a Second Temple commonplace the author and his hearers knew. Verbal volume (logos + sharp sword + active power) is high for an allusion; scholars (Beale & Carson) flag it as the proximate background.

echoes.text: You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for Yahweh searches all hearts, and understands all the imaginations of the thoughts.
echoes.note: ‘Able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart’ (v. 12) restates the OT axiom that God ‘searches all hearts and understands every imagination of the thoughts.’ Thematic coherence is exact; the link is conceptual rather than verbatim, so allusion. The agent shifts from ‘Yahweh’ to ‘the word of God,’ which then resolves into ‘his sight… to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13).

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: A second witness to the heart-searching God who judges ‘according to his ways’ — coherent with Hebrews' ‘him to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13). Like 1 Chr 28:9 it supplies the conceptual substrate for the word that ‘discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart’; no verbal quotation, hence allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh looks from heaven. He sees all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions all of their hearts; and he considers all of their works.
echoes.note: ‘There is no creature that is hidden from his sight’ (v. 13) echoes the psalmist's God who from heaven ‘sees all the sons of men… considers all their works.’ Low verbal volume; the coherence is the all-seeing, work-weighing gaze before which nothing is concealed.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: The classic psalm of the inescapable, all-knowing gaze — God who knows the thought ‘from afar’ and every word ‘on my tongue.’ Faint and uncited, but thematically the nearest psalmic parallel to ‘no creature hidden from his sight… all things naked and laid open’ (vv. 12–13).

echoes.text: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
echoes.note: The striking word ‘naked’ (gymna) before God in v. 13 has a faint precursor in the wisdom topos that even Sheol lies ‘naked’ and ‘uncovered’ before God. Verbal volume rests on the single image of nakedness/exposure; widely noted as a faint echo (NA28/UBS margin).

echoes.text: Sheol and Abaddon are before Yahweh—how much more then the hearts of the children of men!
echoes.note: Parallel to Job 26:6, and closer still to Hebrews' move from cosmic exposure to the human heart: if Sheol lies open, ‘how much more the hearts of men.’ A faint a-fortiori echo behind ‘naked and laid open… the thoughts and intentions of the heart.’

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: ‘Having then a great high priest… Jesus, the Son of God’ (v. 14) introduces, without citation, the high-priestly theme grounded in Ps 110:4 (quoted at 5:6; 7:17) — the verse that controls the whole central argument. No verbal volume here, but high recurrence in Hebrews makes the figural anticipation audible: the transition from the searching word to the sympathetic priest is the book's hinge.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: The priest ‘who has passed through the heavens’ and the invitation to ‘draw near… to the throne of grace’ (vv. 14, 16) presuppose the enthronement of Ps 110:1, the catena's bracket (1:13; 10:12). Faint and figural — the throne-of-grace language assumes the session at the right hand the letter has already established.

pericopes.text: For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness. Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself. Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was.

echoes.text: “Bring Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, near to you from among the children of Israel, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office, even Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s sons.
echoes.note: ‘He is called by God, just like Aaron’ (v. 4) names Aaron's installation directly; Exod 28:1 is the foundational text where God ‘brings near’ Aaron to the priesthood. Moderate verbal volume (the proper name Aaron is shared) plus high thematic coherence with the high-priest argument seeded since 2:17 (Hays' recurrence).

echoes.text: to be a memorial to the children of Israel, to the end that no stranger, who isn’t of the offspring of Aaron, would come near to burn incense before Yahweh, that he not be as Korah, and as his company; as Yahweh spoke to him by Moses.
echoes.note: ‘Nobody takes this honor on himself’ (v. 4) recalls the Korah rebellion (Num 16–17), the locus classicus for seizing priesthood uninvited; the bronze-censer memorial of 16:40 warns against the ‘stranger’ who presumes. No verbatim quotation — a thematic allusion to the negative type behind Hebrews' rule of divine calling.

echoes.text: Moses said to Aaron, “Draw near to the altar, and offer your sin offering, and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself, and for the people; and offer the offering of the people, and make atonement for them; as Yahweh commanded.”
echoes.note: ‘He must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself’ (v. 3) compresses the cultic logic of Lev 9:7, where Aaron atones first ‘for yourself’ then ‘for the people.’ Verbal coherence (the doubled for-himself/for-the-people structure) marks this as the underlying script; the divergence Hebrews exploits is that Christ, sinless (4:15; 7:27), needs no offering for himself.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and for his house.
echoes.note: The Day-of-Atonement requirement that the high priest atone ‘for himself’ (Lev 16:6) undergirds v. 3 and is the foil Hebrews overturns at 7:27. A faint echo paralleling Lev 9:7; recurrence of the Lev 16 figure already running through the letter (1:3; 9:7) raises its credence (Hays).

pericopes.text: So also Christ didn't glorify himself to be made a high priest, but it was he who said to him, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father.’ As he says also in another place, ‘You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.’ He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear, though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation, named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’
echoes.note: Re-cited from 1:5, now welded to priesthood: the same divine ‘today’ that enthrones the Son also installs him as high priest. Recurrence binding the two halves of the letter together.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: The hinge of the whole letter. Ps 110:1 crowned the Son at 1:13; now verse 4 of the same psalm makes him priest — a priesthood older than Aaron's, sworn by an oath. Named here, expounded at length in chapter 7.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
echoes.note: The name ‘Melchizedek’ (vv. 6, 10) points beyond Ps 110:4 to its narrative root in Gen 14:18, the only other Old Testament Melchizedek text and the one ch. 7 will expound at length. The repeated naming is Hays' recurrence in advance — the figure is planted here and harvested in chapter 7.

echoes.text: For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, Neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard.
echoes.note: ‘Strong crying… having been heard for his godly fear’ (v. 7) reads the righteous sufferer's vindication: the very psalm of the cross (Ps 22, already cited at 2:12) testifies that God ‘heard’ the afflicted one's cry. Thematic coherence and recurrence of Ps 22 in Hebrews make this a heard, if unquoted, link to the Passion.

echoes.text: I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy. Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live. The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: ‘Prayers and petitions… to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard’ (v. 7) closely tracks the lament-deliverance pattern of Ps 116: encircled by the ‘cords of death,’ the petitioner cries and is heard. Scholars (Beale & Carson) hear the Gethsemane prayer voiced through the lament psalms; medium volume, strong thematic fit.

echoes.text: “Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry. Don’t be silent at my tears. For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.
echoes.note: ‘With strong crying and tears’ (v. 7) — the explicit ‘tears’ — faintly echoes the lament topos of Ps 39:12, where the sufferer begs God not to ‘be silent at my tears.’ Low verbal volume and a contested identification (any lament psalm could supply the motif), included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: You shall not go out from the door of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your consecration are fulfilled: for he shall consecrate you seven days.
echoes.note: ‘Having been made perfect’ (teleiōtheis, v. 9) carries the cultic sense of priestly ‘perfecting/consecration’ — the LXX teleioō word-group renders the ‘fill the hand’ ordination of Lev 8 (cf. 8:33, the seven-day consecration). A faint figural link: Christ's perfecting through suffering reworks the priest's installation rite. LXX-specific; invisible in the Hebrew ‘fill the hands.’

pericopes.text: About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret, seeing you have become dull of hearing. For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food. For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby. But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.

echoes.text: Whom will he teach knowledge? To whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts?
echoes.note: The milk-versus-maturity reproach (vv. 12–13) faintly echoes Isaiah's taunt that only the ‘weaned from the milk’ can receive teaching. Low verbal volume — the milk/solid-food trope is a wisdom commonplace (cf. 1 Cor 3:1–2) — but Isa 28:9 is the nearest scriptural antecedent of teaching figured as feeding. Contested as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
echoes.note: ‘Senses exercised to discern good and evil’ (v. 14) reuses the Eden phrase ‘knowing good and evil’ (Gen 2–3). Probably an idiom of moral maturity rather than a pointed citation, but the verbal pair is verbatim with the Genesis tree; included as a faint, contested figural-tinged echo for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: Therefore leaving the teaching of the first principles of Christ, let us press on to perfection—not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works, of faith toward God, of the teaching of baptisms, of laying on of hands, of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. This will we do, if God permits. For concerning those who were once enlightened and tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the age to come, and then fell away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance; seeing they crucify the Son of God for themselves again, and put him to open shame. For the land which has drunk the rain that comes often on it, and produces a crop suitable for them for whose sake it is also tilled, receives blessing from God; but if it bears thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near being cursed, whose end is to be burned.

echoes.text: To Adam he said, ‘Because you have listened to your wife's voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, “You shall not eat of it,” the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.’
echoes.note: ‘Bears thorns and thistles… near being cursed’ (v. 8) is a high-volume verbal allusion: the exact pairing ‘thorns and thistles’ (akanthas kai tribolous) plus the verb ‘cursed’ reproduces the Edenic curse on the ground. The LXX of Gen 3:18 reads the same word-pair Hebrews uses, so the verbal volume is strongest against the Greek. Thematic coherence: fruitless ground under divine curse is exactly the apostate's end.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the middle of it, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes... I will lay it a wasteland. It won't be pruned nor hoed, but it will grow briers and thorns. I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain on it.
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard underwrites the whole 6:7–8 figure: cultivated ground that, despite the owner's labor and rain, yields only thorns and is given over to ruin. Hays' thematic coherence is strong (well-tilled land judged by its fruit; rain withheld), and ‘briers and thorns’ recurs as the marker of covenant failure (cf. Isa 7:23–25).

echoes.text: but the land, where you go over to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys which drinks water from the rain of the sky,
echoes.note: ‘The land which has drunk the rain… receives blessing from God’ (v. 7) echoes the Deuteronomic land that ‘drinks water from the rain of the sky’ — the blessing-or-curse alternative set before Israel (Deut 11:11–17, 26–28). Low verbal volume (the verb ‘drink the rain’ is the hinge), but high thematic coherence: fertility as covenant blessing, drought as curse.

echoes.text: because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.
echoes.note: The portrait of those ‘once enlightened… and then fell away’ whom it is ‘impossible to renew to repentance’ (vv. 4–6) recurs to the wilderness generation that saw God's glory and signs yet was barred from the land — the same exemplum Hebrews built in 3:7–4:11 (Hays' recurrence test across the homily). Conceptual, not verbatim.

echoes.text: and that all of its land is sulfur, salt, and burning, that it is not sown, doesn't produce, nor does any grass grow in it, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which Yahweh overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath;
echoes.note: ‘Whose end is to be burned’ (v. 8) faintly recalls the Deuteronomic curse of a barren, burning land that ‘doesn't produce.’ Verbal volume is low (the shared note is land that yields nothing and is consigned to burning), but the covenant blessing/curse frame coheres with the field imagery; flagged contested.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The catechetical pair ‘resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment’ (v. 2) draws on the apocalyptic two-outcome resurrection of Dan 12:2 (life vs. everlasting contempt). Faint and topical rather than verbal — these were stock elements of early Jewish-Christian instruction — but Daniel is its clearest scriptural anchor.

pericopes.text: But, beloved, we are persuaded of better things for you, and things that accompany salvation, even though we speak like this. For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them. We desire that each one of you may show the same diligence to the fullness of hope even to the end, that you won't be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: ‘God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love… you served the saints’ (v. 10) sounds the wisdom axiom that mercy to the needy is a loan God repays. Low verbal volume and contested, but the theme — God's unfailing reward of ministry to others — coheres, and the formula reappears in the ‘rewarder’ of 11:6.

echoes.text: and said, ‘I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore.’
echoes.note: ‘Imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises’ (v. 12) anticipates Abraham, named immediately in v. 13 as the one who, ‘having patiently endured, obtained the promise.’ The echo is the seam that joins the warning to the Abraham oath of the next pericope (Hays' recurrence — the same exemplar carries across the paragraph break).

pericopes.text: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself, saying, ‘Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.’ Thus, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise. For men indeed swear by a greater one, and in every dispute of theirs the oath is final for confirmation. In this way God, being determined to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed with an oath; that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have a strong encouragement, who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before us. This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil; where as a forerunner Jesus entered for us, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

echoes.text: and said, ‘I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore.’
echoes.note: God's oath to Abraham at the binding of Isaac — sworn ‘by myself’ because there is none greater. Hebrews seizes on the oath itself: God condescends to swear, so the promise rests on ‘two immutable things’ (v. 18), his word and his oath.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: The chapter closes by sounding Melchizedek again (v. 20), the cue for the full exposition in ch. 7. Recurrence threading the priesthood theme through a warning passage.

echoes.text: and Yahweh said to Moses, ‘Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.’
echoes.note: ‘Entering into that which is within the veil’ (v. 19) names the inner sanctum that Lev 16 reserves for the high priest on the Day of Atonement alone. Hebrews reads the veil figurally as the boundary Jesus crossed once for all ‘as a forerunner’ — the same Day-of-Atonement typology seeded at 1:3 and expounded in chs. 9–10 (Hays' recurrence and figural coherence).

echoes.text: You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil: and the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.
echoes.note: The tabernacle veil ‘within’ which the ark stood is the architectural referent of ‘within the veil’ (v. 19). Hebrews' word katapetasma matches the LXX term for this dividing curtain; the figure of the believer's hope as an anchor reaching past the veil presupposes the two-roomed sanctuary of Exod 26 (cf. the same veil at Heb 9:3; 10:20).

echoes.text: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?
echoes.note: ‘It is impossible for God to lie’ (v. 18) restates Balaam's axiom that God, unlike a man, cannot lie or repent of his word. Conceptual allusion (no shared catchword), but the thought is verbatim in substance and undergirds the ‘two immutable things’ argument; the divine truthfulness theme returns at Heb 10:23 and Titus 1:2.

echoes.text: Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.
echoes.note: A second witness to the same maxim behind ‘impossible for God to lie’ (v. 18): the Glory/Strength of Israel ‘will not lie nor repent.’ Paired with Num 23:19 as the gezerah-shavah-style backdrop (the immutability of God's sworn counsel), though here verbal volume is low and the link is contested.

echoes.text: The congregation shall deliver the man slayer out of the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge, where he had fled.
echoes.note: ‘We who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope’ (v. 18) faintly evokes the cities of refuge to which the manslayer ‘fled’ and was held safe ‘until the high priest dies’ — a poignant counterpoint, since here safety comes through the high priest who lives forever (v. 20). Low volume and contested; some read only a general ‘flee for refuge’ idiom.

pericopes.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom also Abraham divided a tenth part of all (being first, by interpretation, ‘king of righteousness’, and then also ‘king of Salem’, which means ‘king of peace’; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God), remains a priest continually. Now consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham, the patriarch, gave a tenth out of the best plunder. They indeed of the sons of Levi who receive the priest's office have a commandment to take tithes of the people according to the law, that is, of their brothers, though these have come out of the body of Abraham, but he whose genealogy is not counted from them has accepted tithes from Abraham, and has blessed him who has the promises. But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater. Here people who die receive tithes, but there one receives tithes of whom it is testified that he lives. We can say that through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, has paid tithes, for he was yet in the body of his father when Melchizedek met him.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High. He blessed him, and said, ‘Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth:’ and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.' Abram gave him a tenth of all.
echoes.note: The argument reads the silences of the Genesis story figurally: Melchizedek enters with no genealogy, no birth, no death on record, so ‘he remains a priest continually’ — a figure of an eternal priesthood. Classic figural reasoning from what the narrative does not say. Even the names are mined: Melchizedek = ‘king of righteousness,’ Salem = ‘peace.’

echoes.text: The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley).
echoes.note: ‘Who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings’ (v. 1) lifts the narrative frame verbatim from the verse immediately preceding the Melchizedek scene. High verbal volume on the ‘slaughter of the kings’ phrase; the surrounding verses (14:18–20) are the figural core, so this opening clause is a near-quotation supplying the setting.

echoes.text: To the children of Levi, behold, I have given all the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service which they serve, even the service of the Tent of Meeting.
echoes.note: ‘The sons of Levi… have a commandment to take tithes of the people according to the law’ (v. 5) alludes directly to the Levitical tithe-statute. Strong thematic coherence: the whole pericope contrasts the Levites who receive tithes by legal mandate with Melchizedek, who received them from Abraham himself, the Levites' ancestor. Verbal overlap on ‘tithe’ and ‘the children of Levi.’

echoes.text: His tabernacle is also in Salem; His dwelling place in Zion.
echoes.note: The gloss ‘king of Salem, which means king of peace’ trades on the identification of Salem with Zion/Jerusalem found at Ps 76:2, the one other place Scripture names ‘Salem.’ Modest verbal volume (the shared toponym) but high thematic coherence — it licenses the peace etymology (Salem/shalom) on which the wordplay depends.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: ‘Remains a priest continually’ (v. 3) reads the Genesis silences through the lens of Ps 110:4, the verse this whole chapter expounds — the eternal Melchizedekian priesthood. Recurrence is decisive (Hays): the psalm is quoted explicitly at vv. 17 and 21, so its perpetuity language is already audible here in the figural portrait.

pericopes.text: Now if there were perfection through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people have received the law), what further need was there for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, and not be called after the order of Aaron? For the priesthood being changed, there is of necessity a change made also in the law. For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one has officiated at the altar.
