For it is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah, about which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning priesthood. This is yet more abundantly evident, if after the likeness of Melchizedek there arises another priest, who has been made, not after the law of a fleshly commandment, but after the power of an endless life: for it is testified, ‘You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.’ For there is an annulling of a foregoing commandment because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect), and a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: Quoted as proof (v. 17) that a priesthood ‘after the order of Melchizedek’ — not Aaron's — was always promised. If the priesthood changes, Hebrews argues, the law itself must change with it: the letter's most radical claim, carried by a single verse.

echoes.text: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs; and to him will the obedience of the peoples be.
echoes.note: ‘It is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah’ (v. 14) presupposes the Judah-tribe messianism of Jacob's blessing — the scepter that ‘will not depart from Judah.’ No verbatim citation (a dashed allusion), but high thematic coherence: the argument needs a Messiah from a non-priestly tribe, and Gen 49:10 is the locus classicus for the ruler from Judah.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The Davidic-from-Judah origin (‘sprung out of Judah,’ v. 14) faintly sounds the Jesse/David shoot of Isa 11:1. Low verbal volume — the link is conceptual (Messiah from Judah's royal line, not Levi) — but it reinforces the same tribal-displacement logic the pericope is pressing.

echoes.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.
echoes.note: A faint, contested echo: ‘our Lord has sprung out of Judah’ overlaps with Micah's ‘ruler in Israel’ coming ‘out of’ Bethlehem-in-Judah. Very low volume and no verbal contact beyond the Judah-origin theme; included for maximal coverage where scholars list Judah-Messiah testimonia.

echoes.text: To the children of Levi, behold, I have given all the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service which they serve, even the service of the Tent of Meeting.
echoes.note: The ‘Levitical priesthood… under which the people received the law’ (v. 11) and the contrast with a priest from a tribe that never ‘officiated at the altar’ (v. 13) presuppose the Levi-only priestly charter of Numbers 18. Recurrence within the chapter (the same statute underlies 7:5) raises confidence on an otherwise conceptual allusion.

pericopes.text: Inasmuch as he was not made priest without the taking of an oath (for they indeed have been made priests without an oath), but he with an oath by him that says of him, ‘The Lord swore and will not change his mind, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”’ By so much, Jesus has become the collateral of a better covenant. Many, indeed, have been made priests, because they are hindered from continuing by death. But he, because he lives forever, has his priesthood unchangeable. Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them. For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, guiltless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who doesn't need, like those high priests, to offer up sacrifices daily, first for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once for all, when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men as high priests who have weakness, but the word of the oath which came after the law appoints a Son forever who has been perfected.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: Now the weight falls on the psalm's opening words — ‘The Lord swore and will not change his mind.’ The Levites became priests without an oath; this priest is sworn in by God, so his is the ‘better covenant.’ The same verse, re-read for its oath (recurrence).

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I give him a portion with the great, and he will divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: ‘He lives forever to make intercession for them’ (v. 25) and ‘to offer… for the sins of the people… he offered up himself’ (vv. 27) echo the Suffering Servant who ‘made intercession for the transgressors’ and ‘bore the sin of many.’ Verbal contact on ‘intercession’ and ‘sins of many / bear sin’; thematic coherence with Hebrews' self-offering priest is strong even without a citation formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Made higher than the heavens’ (v. 26) faintly sounds the session-at-the-right-hand of Ps 110:1, the psalm's first verse paired throughout Hebrews with its fourth (1:13; 8:1; 10:12). Low volume here, but recurrence across the letter makes even the faint exaltation language audible as Ps 110:1.

echoes.text: for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘He did this once for all, when he offered up himself’ (v. 27), set against high priests who ‘offer up sacrifices daily… first for his own sins,’ figurally invokes the Day of Atonement (Lev 16), the cult expounded in chs 9–10. No quotation; the once-versus-repeated, self-offering-versus-for-his-own-sins contrast is the borrowed pattern. The motif recurs from 1:3 onward (Hays' recurrence).

pericopes.text: Now in the things which we are saying, the main point is this. We have such a high priest, who sat down on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a servant of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, not man. For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it is necessary that this high priest also have something to offer. For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, seeing there are priests who offer the gifts according to the law; who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle, for he said, ‘See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.’ But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by so much as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which on better promises has been given as law.

echoes.text: See that you make them after their pattern, which has been shown to you on the mountain.
echoes.note: God's instruction to Moses — build the tabernacle to the ‘pattern shown on the mountain’ — becomes Hebrews' warrant that the earthly sanctuary is only a ‘copy and shadow’ of a heavenly original. One verse turns Israel's tent into a replica of things in the heavens.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Who sat down on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens’ (v. 1) sounds Ps 110:1 once more — the session-oracle that bracketed chapter 1 (1:3, 1:13) and recurs at 10:12. By Hays' recurrence test the saturation of Ps 110 through Hebrews makes even this unmarked allusion certain; here it is fused with the priesthood of Ps 110:4 so that the same enthroned Lord is the heavenly high priest.

echoes.text: You shall set up the tabernacle according to the way that it was shown to you on the mountain.
echoes.note: The ‘pattern on the mountain’ motif Hebrews quotes (8:5) is not isolated to Exod 25:40 but recurs across the tabernacle instructions (Exod 25:9; 26:30; 27:8), and the LXX typos (‘pattern/type’) is precisely the word Hebrews exploits. Recurrence within the source itself strengthens the figural reading; medium volume because it is the cluster, not this single verse, that is heard.

echoes.text: As valleys they are spread out, as gardens by the riverside, as aloes which Yahweh has planted, as cedar trees beside the waters.
echoes.note: ‘The true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched (epēxen), not man’ (v. 2) faintly echoes Balaam's oracle, where the LXX of Num 24:6 reads ‘tents which the Lord pitched’ (skēnai has epēxen Kyrios) — the same rare verb for God, not man, pitching the tent. Low verbal volume and contested, but scholars (Attridge) note the lexical link; flagged because the echo lives only in the Greek.

echoes.text: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far away from the camp, and he called it ‘The Tent of Meeting.’
echoes.note: The contrast between the ‘true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, not man’ (v. 2) and the human tent of meeting Moses himself pitched (Exod 33:7) is a faint thematic echo: the wilderness tent, set up by a man, is the very ‘copy and shadow’ Hebrews relativizes. Thematic coherence rather than verbal volume; a contested, low-volume link.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: ‘He is also the mediator of a better covenant, which on better promises has been given as law’ (v. 6) pre-echoes the Jeremiah ‘new covenant’ oracle the very next pericope quotes in full (8:8–12). Hays' recurrence and satisfaction tests: the keyword ‘covenant… better’ seeds the citation about to dominate, so the faint anticipation is heard in retrospect.

pericopes.text: For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second. For finding fault with them, he said, ‘Behold, the days come’, says the Lord, ‘that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they didn't continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them,’ says the Lord. ‘For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel. After those days,’ says the Lord; ‘I will put my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people. They will not teach every man his fellow citizen, and every man his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” for all will know me, from their least to their greatest. For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness. I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.’ In that he says, ‘A new covenant’, he has made the first old. But that which is becoming old and grows aged is near to vanishing away.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them, says Yahweh. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people. They will no longer each teach his neighbor, and every man teach his brother, saying, ‘Know Yahweh;’ for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
echoes.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament. Hebrews lets Jeremiah's promise of a ‘new’ covenant do the demolition: the mere word ‘new’ pronounces the first ‘old… near to vanishing.’ Re-cited in part at 10:16–17 to bracket the central argument.

echoes.text: “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Flagged as a textual fork within the quotation: where the Hebrew of Jer 31:32 reads ‘although I was a husband to them (or: their master),’ the LXX Hebrews follows reads ‘and I disregarded them’ (ēmelēsa) — the rendering printed at 8:9. A classic Greek-vs-Hebrew divergence (Beale & Carson) carried inside the long citation; included separately to mark the seam Hebrews' argument leans on.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.’
echoes.note: ‘The covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt’ (v. 9) points, through Jeremiah's words, back to the Sinai covenant ratified in blood at Exod 24:8 — the ‘first covenant’ Hebrews names as now ‘old.’ Thematic coherence with the blood-of-the-covenant argument Hebrews makes explicit at 9:18–20; faint here, low volume.

pericopes.text: Now indeed even the first covenant had ordinances of divine service, and an earthly sanctuary. For a tabernacle was prepared. In the first part were the lamp stand, the table, and the show bread; which is called the Holy Place. After the second veil was the tabernacle which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden altar of incense, and the ark of the covenant overlaid on all sides with gold, in which was a golden pot holding the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant; and above it cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, of which things we can't speak now in detail. Now these things having been thus prepared, the priests go in continually into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the services, but into the second the high priest alone, once in the year, not without blood, which he offers for himself, and for the errors of the people. The Holy Spirit is indicating this, that the way into the Holy Place wasn't yet revealed while the first tabernacle was still standing; which is a symbol of the present age, where gifts and sacrifices are offered that are incapable, concerning the conscience, of making the worshiper perfect; being only (with meats and drinks and various washings) fleshly ordinances, imposed until a time of reformation.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: The two-roomed tabernacle and ‘the high priest alone, once in the year, not without blood’ (v. 7) describe the Day of Atonement (Lev 16). Hebrews reads the very architecture figurally — the veil barring the way in is ‘the Holy Spirit indicating’ that access to God was not yet open. The figure first heard at 1:3 now becomes the argument.

echoes.text: and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.
echoes.note: ‘Into the second the high priest alone, once in the year’ (v. 7) restates the controlling restriction of Lev 16:2 — entry behind the veil only on the one prescribed day. High thematic coherence and verbal volume (‘within the veil… mercy seat… ark’); the prohibition is precisely the ‘way not yet revealed’ Hebrews exploits (v. 8).

echoes.text: He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times. “Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering, that is for the people, and bring his blood within the veil, and do with his blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy seat, and before the mercy seat.
echoes.note: ‘Not without blood, which he offers for himself, and for the errors of the people’ (v. 7) compresses the bull-for-himself / goat-for-the-people sequence of Lev 16:14–15. Recurrence within Hebrews (the same blood-rite returns at 9:25) and thematic coherence support the link, though no clause is quoted verbatim.

echoes.text: You shall make a lamp stand of pure gold. Of hammered work shall the lamp stand be made, even its base, its shaft, its cups, its buds, and its flowers, shall be of one piece with it. There shall be six branches going out of its sides... You shall make its lamps seven, and they shall light its lamps to give light to the space in front of it.
echoes.note: ‘The lamp stand’ in the first room (v. 2) names the menorah commanded in Exod 25:31–37. Verbal volume is a single furnishing word, but the whole catalogue of vv. 2–5 systematically recapitulates the Exodus tabernacle inventory — recurrence across furnishings makes each item's source secure.

echoes.text: “You shall make a table of acacia wood... You shall overlay it with pure gold, and make a gold molding around it... You shall set bread of the presence on the table before me always.
echoes.note: ‘The table, and the show bread’ (v. 2) draw on the table of the Presence in Exod 25:23–30 (‘bread of the presence… before me always’). Part of the running tabernacle-inventory allusion; thematic coherence is exact even where verbal contact is just the furnishing names.

echoes.text: “You shall make an altar to burn incense on. You shall make it of acacia wood... You shall overlay it with pure gold... You shall put it before the veil that is by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat that is over the testimony, where I will meet with you.
echoes.note: ‘A golden altar of incense’ (v. 4) recalls Exod 30:1–6. Contested because Exod 30:6 locates the incense altar before the veil (in the Holy Place), while Hebrews places it with the inner room — a famous topographical divergence the author may be following the LXX/Second-Temple tradition on. The verbal echo ‘golden… altar of incense’ is strong; the placement is the crux.
echoes.altSource: Leviticus 16:12–13 (incense within the veil on the Day of Atonement)

echoes.text: You shall put the testimony which I shall give you into the ark.
echoes.note: ‘The tablets of the covenant’ inside the ark (v. 4) answer Exod 25:16 (‘put the testimony… into the ark’). High thematic coherence; the ‘testimony’ = the tablets, which Hebrews lists among the ark's contents.

echoes.text: Moses said to Aaron, “Take a pot, and put an omer-full of manna in it, and lay it up before Yahweh, to be kept throughout your generations.”
echoes.note: ‘A golden pot holding the manna’ (v. 4) draws on Exod 16:33. The LXX adds ‘golden’ (the Hebrew says only ‘a pot’), so Hebrews follows the Greek detail — an availability/divergence point. Strong thematic coherence with the ark's stored memorials.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Put back the rod of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept for a token against the children of rebellion; that you may make an end of their murmurings against me, that they not die.”
echoes.note: ‘Aaron's rod that budded’ (v. 4) recalls Num 17:10, where the rod is laid up ‘before the testimony’ as a token. Together with the manna pot and tablets it completes the ark's contents; recurrence of the storage formula (‘before the testimony / before Yahweh’) ties the three memorials together.

echoes.text: You shall make two cherubim of hammered gold... The cherubim shall spread out their wings upward, covering the mercy seat with their wings... There I will meet with you, and I will tell you from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim which are on the ark of the testimony.
echoes.note: ‘Cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat’ (v. 5) is verbally dense with Exod 25:18–22 (‘cherubim… covering the mercy seat with their wings’). High volume on ‘cherubim’ + ‘mercy seat’; this is the closest-to-quotation of the inventory allusions.

echoes.text: “You shall make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim... the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.
echoes.note: ‘After the second veil’ (v. 3) presupposes Exod 26:31–33, the veil that ‘separates the holy place from the most holy.’ Hebrews' phrase ‘second veil’ reflects the two-curtain reading of the tent; the dividing-veil that bars the way in is the load-bearing image for v. 8.

echoes.text: So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.
echoes.note: A faint, contested figural undertone: cherubim ‘overshadowing’ and a veil that bars ‘the way into the Holy Place’ (v. 8) recall the cherubim who ‘guard the way’ to Eden's tree of life (Gen 3:24). Low verbal volume and no recurrence in Hebrews, but some readers (Hays-style figural coherence) hear the blocked-access motif of paradise behind the closed sanctuary.

pericopes.text: But Christ having come as a high priest of the coming good things, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation, nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant, that those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where a last will and testament is, there must of necessity be the death of him who made it. For a will is in force where there has been death, for it is never in force while he who made it lives. Therefore even the first covenant has not been dedicated without blood. For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves and the goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.’ Moreover he sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry in the same way with the blood. According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.’
echoes.note: Moses' words at Sinai, inaugurating the first covenant in blood. Hebrews quotes them to make blood the necessary seal of any covenant — and so to read Christ's death as the blood that ratifies the new one: ‘apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.’

echoes.text: Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar. He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that Yahweh has spoken will we do, and be obedient.” Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: Beyond the quoted clause (v. 8), the whole narrative frame of vv. 19–20 — Moses reading ‘every commandment to all the people,’ then sprinkling — retells Exod 24:6–8. Hebrews adds details (water, scarlet wool, hyssop, sprinkling the book) not in Exod 24, conflating it with the purification rites (Num 19; Lev 14): high recurrence of the sprinkling motif drives the link.

echoes.text: “A man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay them up outside of the camp in a clean place; and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for use in water for cleansing impurity. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: ‘The ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled’ (v. 13) names the red-heifer rite of Num 19:9. Strong verbal volume (‘ashes of the heifer… cleansing impurity’) and exact thematic coherence: an outward cleansing ‘of the flesh’ that Hebrews contrasts with the inward cleansing of conscience by Christ's blood.

echoes.text: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there...
echoes.note: The mechanics of v. 13 (ashes + water sprinkled on the defiled) and the ‘water… and hyssop’ of vv. 19–21 echo Num 19:17–18, where hyssop dips the ash-water and sprinkles ‘the tent, all the vessels, the persons.’ Hebrews' phrase ‘sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels’ tracks this list closely — recurrence of sprinkling vocabulary.

echoes.text: The priest shall take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet, and cast it into the middle of the burning of the heifer.
echoes.note: ‘With water and scarlet wool and hyssop’ (v. 19) imports the ‘hyssop and scarlet’ of the heifer rite (Num 19:6) into the retelling of the Sinai covenant-cutting, which had neither. The conflation shows Hebrews reading all the blood-rites as one figural system; verbal contact on ‘scarlet… hyssop’ is the tell.
echoes.altSource: Leviticus 14:4–6 (scarlet and hyssop in the cleansing of the leper)

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: ‘Apart from shedding of blood there is no remission’ (v. 22) crystallizes the principle of Lev 17:11 — blood makes atonement because the life is in it. No verbatim quotation, but high thematic coherence: this is the axiom on which the whole sacrificial argument of vv. 11–22 rests.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘The blood of goats and calves’ / ‘goats and bulls’ (vv. 12–13, 19) generalizes the Day-of-Atonement victims (bull and goat, Lev 16:3, 5–15). Faint and diffuse — Hebrews blends Day-of-Atonement animals with covenant-inauguration animals (Exod 24) — so verbal volume is low and the source is one strand among several.

pericopes.text: It was necessary therefore that the copies of the things in the heavens should be cleansed with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ hasn't entered into holy places made with hands, which are representations of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us; nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy place year by year with blood not his own, or else he must have suffered often since the foundation of the world. But now once at the end of the ages, he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this, judgment, so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, to those who are eagerly waiting for him for salvation.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: The Day-of-Atonement figure reaches its payoff: where the high priest ‘enters the holy place year by year,’ Christ enters heaven itself ‘once at the end of the ages.’ The whole typology turns on once versus yearly — the repeated rite was always pointing past itself to a single, final sacrifice.

echoes.text: Therefore will I give him a portion with the great, and he will divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: ‘Having been offered once to bear the sins of many’ (v. 28) verbally echoes Isa 53:12, ‘he bore the sin of many.’ The Greek of Isaiah (anēnenken hamartias pollōn) overlaps Hebrews' wording closely — high verbal volume for an allusion, and thematic coherence with the suffering servant who ‘poured out his soul to death.’ The only Servant-Song echo in the letter, which makes it contested by the recurrence test even as the verbal volume is strong.

echoes.text: “This shall be an everlasting statute for you, to make atonement for the children of Israel once in the year because of all their sins.”
echoes.note: ‘As the high priest enters into the holy place year by year’ (v. 25) restates the ‘once in the year’ statute of Lev 16:34. The contrast Hebrews builds (yearly repetition vs. Christ's single entry) hangs on this annual cadence; verbal contact on ‘once in the year.’

echoes.text: He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times. “Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering, that is for the people, and bring his blood within the veil, and do with his blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy seat, and before the mercy seat.
echoes.note: ‘With blood not his own’ (v. 25) points to the bull-and-goat blood the high priest carries within the veil in Lev 16:14–15 — ‘blood not his own’ in contrast to Christ's self-offering. An echo (the rite is presupposed, not quoted); recurrence of the same Lev 16 blood-entry across 9:7, 9:12, and here.

echoes.text: [allusive phrase] ‘since the foundation of the world’ (v. 26), echoing the primeval frame of creation and the first sin in Genesis 2–3.
echoes.note: ‘Or else he must have suffered often since the foundation of the world’ (v. 26) is a faint temporal echo reaching back to creation and the entrance of sin (Gen 2–3). No quotation and no fetched verse anchors a single line; included as a low-confidence figural horizon under Hays' criterion of thematic coherence, since Hebrews dates the once-for-all offering against the whole span ‘from the foundation of the world.’

pericopes.text: For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near. Or else wouldn't they have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, having been once cleansed, would have had no more consciousness of sins? But in those sacrifices there is a yearly reminder of sins. For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins. Therefore when he comes into the world, he says, ‘Sacrifice and offering you didn't desire, but you prepared a body for me. You had no pleasure in whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin. Then I said, “Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God.”’ Previously saying, ‘Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you didn't desire, neither had pleasure in them’ (those which are offered according to the law), then he has said, ‘Behold, I have come to do your will.’ He takes away the first, that he may establish the second, by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

echoes.text: Sacrifice and offering you didn’t desire. You have opened my ears. You have not required burnt offering and sin offering. Then I said, “Behold, I have come. It is written about me in the book in the scroll. I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”
echoes.note: Another Greek/Hebrew fork, and the most consequential one. Where the Hebrew reads ‘ears you have opened (dug),’ the Septuagint that Hebrews quotes reads ‘a body you prepared for me’ — and on that ‘body’ the whole argument of the once-for-all bodily offering turns (v. 10). Availability again: the author's Bible was the Greek.
echoes.lxxText: Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not; but a body hast thou prepared me: whole-burnt-offering and sacrifice for sin thou didst not require. Then I said, Behold, I come: in the volume of the book it is written concerning me, I desired to do thy will, O my God, and thy law in the midst of mine heart.

echoes.text: This shall be an everlasting statute for you, to make atonement for the children of Israel once in the year because of all their sins.
echoes.note: ‘The same sacrifices year by year… a yearly reminder of sins’ (vv. 1, 3) presupposes the once-a-year Day of Atonement statute. High thematic coherence with the book's central typology (chs 9–10): the very repetition Leviticus commands is what Hebrews turns into proof of the law's inability to perfect.

echoes.text: "What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?", says Yahweh. "I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed animals. I don't delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of male goats.
echoes.note: The prophetic critique of mere sacrifice stands behind both Ps 40 and Hebrews' gloss. ‘The blood of bulls and goats’ (v. 4) sounds Isaiah's ‘blood of bulls… and of male goats’ — thematic coherence (Hays) with the prophets' sacrifice-vs-obedience polemic, even if the verbal volume is faint and mediated through the psalm.

echoes.text: Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh's voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: Samuel's ‘to obey is better than sacrifice’ is the classic locus of the obedience-over-offering theme that Ps 40:6–8 versifies and Hebrews exploits (‘I have come to do your will’ replacing ‘sacrifice… you didn't desire’). Conceptual coherence rather than verbal volume; scholars (Beale & Carson) note it as the OT backdrop of the contrast.

echoes.text: For you don't delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
echoes.note: A faint cousin-echo: David's penitential ‘you don't delight in sacrifice… you have no pleasure in burnt offering’ runs verbally parallel to Ps 40's and Hebrews' ‘you didn't desire… had no pleasure.’ Low volume and contested as a direct source, but the shared psalmic formula reinforces the thematic field of sacrifice displaced by the will of the heart.

pericopes.text: Every priest indeed stands day by day serving and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, but he, when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God; from that time waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. The Holy Spirit also testifies to us, for after saying, ‘This is the covenant that I will make with them: “After those days,” says the Lord, “I will put my laws on their heart, I will also write them on their mind;”’ then he says, ‘I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more.’ Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down… waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet’ (vv. 12–13) sounds Ps 110:1 yet again — the seated, finished priest set against the standing priests who never sit, because their work is never done.

echoes.text: I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart... for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's new covenant, quoted in full at 8:8–12, returns here in brief to close the case: if sins are remembered ‘no more,’ then ‘there is no more offering for sin.’ The recurrence brackets the whole central section (Hays).

echoes.text: You shall tell them, ‘This is the offering made by fire which you shall offer to Yahweh: male lambs a year old without defect, two day by day, for a continual burnt offering.
echoes.note: ‘Every priest indeed stands day by day… often offering the same sacrifices’ (v. 11) alludes to the prescribed tamid, the continual daily offering of Num 28. The endless dailiness Numbers legislates is exactly what Hebrews contrasts with Christ's single seated offering — thematic coherence carrying a low-volume allusion.

pericopes.text: Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; and having a great priest over God's house, let's draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and having our body washed with pure water, let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful. Let us consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another; and so much the more, as you see the Day approaching.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your filthiness, and from all your idols.
echoes.note: ‘Hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience… body washed with pure water’ (v. 22) fuses sprinkling and washing exactly as Ezekiel's new-covenant promise of cleansing does. High verbal volume on ‘sprinkle… clean water’; the coherence with the chapter's interior-cleansing argument (cf. 9:13–14) lifts it from echo to allusion.

echoes.text: You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and shall wash them with water.
echoes.note: ‘Body washed with pure water’ figurally extends the priestly consecration of Aaron and his sons (washed with water before approaching). Hebrews makes every believer a priest who ‘draws near’; the priest-ordination rite is the type. Moderate volume, strong typological coherence.

echoes.text: Moses brought Aaron and his sons, and washed them with water.
echoes.note: The narrative enactment of Exod 29:4 — Moses washing Aaron and his sons at their ordination — reinforces the same priestly-washing type behind ‘body washed with pure water.’ Low independent volume; cited by scholars (Beale & Carson) alongside Exod 29 as the consecration backdrop.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The verse immediately following the sprinkling promise: ‘draw near with a true heart’ (v. 22) faintly carries Ezekiel's new-heart language into the same breath as his clean-water language. Low volume, but recurrence of the Ezek 36:25–27 unit in early-Christian new-covenant texts (cf. the Spirit ‘written on hearts’ motif) gives it standing.

echoes.text: and Yahweh said to Moses, ‘Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.’
echoes.note: ‘Boldness to enter into the holy place… through the veil’ (vv. 19–20) inverts the Day-of-Atonement restriction: where Aaron must not come within the veil ‘at all times’ lest he die, believers now have boldness to enter always. Figural reversal of the Lev 16 prohibition — the veil that barred access (cf. 9:8) is now the opened ‘new and living way.’

echoes.text: A man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay them up outside of the camp in a clean place; and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for use in water for cleansing impurity. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: The ‘water for cleansing impurity’ of the red-heifer rite (invoked explicitly at 9:13) lingers behind ‘body washed with pure water.’ Faint and contested as a distinct source here, but Hebrews has already paired heifer-ashes with sprinkling, so the recurrence keeps the lustration imagery in play.

pericopes.text: For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a fierceness of fire which will devour the adversaries. A man who disregards Moses' law dies without compassion on the word of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment do you think he will be judged worthy of who has trodden under foot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant with which he was sanctified an unholy thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, ‘Vengeance belongs to me,’ says the Lord, ‘I will repay.’ Again, ‘The Lord will judge his people.’ It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

echoes.text: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.
echoes.note: From the Song of Moses. ‘Vengeance is mine’ is wielded as warning, not comfort — the same God who saves will judge those who spurn the saving.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will judge his people, and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone; that there is no one remaining, shut up or left at large.
echoes.note: Stitched straight onto the previous line (‘Again…’). ‘The Lord will judge his people’ also stands at Ps 135:14 — two witnesses fused into one verdict.

echoes.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
echoes.note: ‘Dies without compassion on the word of two or three witnesses’ (v. 28) quotes the Deuteronomic evidentiary rule almost verbatim. High verbal volume; the a-fortiori (‘how much worse punishment’) turns the capital-witness statute into the structure of the warning.

echoes.text: Yahweh, your hand is lifted up, yet they don't see; but they will see your zeal for the people, and be disappointed. Yes, fire will consume your adversaries.
echoes.note: ‘A fierceness of fire which will devour the adversaries’ (v. 27) closely follows Isa 26:11 LXX (‘fire will devour the adversaries’). The same Isaiah-26 context supplies 10:37 (‘a little while’), so recurrence within the pericope strengthens the link (Hays); note Hebrews tracks the Greek here.

echoes.text: Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them in the day of Yahweh's wrath, but the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy; for he will make an end, yes, a terrible end, of all those who dwell in the land.
echoes.note: The ‘day of wrath’ devouring fire of Zephaniah feeds the same ‘fierceness of fire’ image. Lower volume than Isa 26:11 and harder to isolate, but the prophetic ‘fire of his jealousy that devours’ is the shared topos commentators cite behind v. 27.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The doublet of Deut 17:6, also phrasing the ‘two or three witnesses’ rule. Either Deuteronomic text could be in view; the recurrence of the formula across the law is itself why Hebrews can treat it as settled procedure.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will judge his people, and have compassion on his servants.
echoes.note: Explicitly flagged in the existing Deut 32:36 note as the alternate locus of ‘The Lord will judge his people.’ Listed in its own right because the wording of Heb 10:30b matches Ps 135:14 as closely as Deut 32:36 — a genuine two-source ambiguity that NA28 margins record.

pericopes.text: But remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle with sufferings; partly, being exposed to both reproaches and oppressions; and partly, becoming partakers with those who were treated so. For you both had compassion on me in my chains, and joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession and an enduring one in the heavens. Therefore don't throw away your boldness, which has a great reward. For you need endurance so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. ‘In a very little while, he who comes will come, and will not wait. But the righteous will live by faith. If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.’ But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul.

echoes.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay. Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: ‘The righteous will live by faith’ — Paul's great text (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11) — here following the Greek, which adds ‘if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.’ It is the hinge into chapter 11: faith defined, then paraded.
echoes.lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry. If he should draw back, my soul has no pleasure in him: but the just shall live by my faith.

echoes.text: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past.
echoes.note: ‘In a very little while’ (v. 37) appears to be a conflated lead-in: Hebrews prefixes Hab 2:3 with the ‘yet a little while’ of Isa 26:20 LXX (‘hide for a little moment until the indignation is past’). The borrowed phrase, and the article on ‘the coming one,’ make the prophecy point to Christ's coming — a Greek-text move (availability/coherence).

pericopes.text: Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen. For by this, the elders obtained testimony. By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible. By faith, Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he had testimony given to him that he was righteous, God testifying with respect to his gifts; and through it he, being dead, still speaks. By faith, Enoch was taken away, so that he wouldn't see death, and he was not found, because God translated him. For he has had testimony given to him that before his translation he had been well pleasing to God. Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. By faith, Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: ‘Enoch… was not found, because God translated him’ retells Gen 5:24, following the Greek (‘transferred’) for the Hebrew ‘God took him.’ The chapter's whole method shows here in miniature — faith demonstrated by retelling the old stories. (Abel and Noah, vv. 4 and 7, are likewise drawn from Genesis 4 and 6–9.)

echoes.text: Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
echoes.note: ‘Abel offered… a more excellent sacrifice than Cain’ (v. 4) retells Gen 4:3–10 — the LORD's ‘respect’ for Abel's offering is read as the testimony ‘that he was righteous.’ High thematic coherence; the narrative is reused whole rather than cited (Hays, figural reading).

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.”
echoes.note: ‘Being dead, he still speaks’ (v. 4) hears Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries from the ground.’ Recurrence clinches it: the same image returns at 12:24 (‘the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’), so even this faint allusion earns its place.

echoes.text: Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch.
echoes.note: ‘Noah… prepared a ship for the saving of his house’ (v. 7) retells the flood narrative of Gen 6–9. The ‘things not yet seen’ are the warned-of flood; Noah's obedience ‘condemned the world.’ The whole story is reused figurally, not quoted.

pericopes.text: By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went. By faith, he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents, with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise. For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God. By faith, even Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she bore a child when she was past age, since she counted him faithful who had promised. Therefore as many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore, were fathered by one man, and him as good as dead. These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own. If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return. But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. By faith, Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac. Yes, he who had gladly received the promises was offering up his one and only son, to whom it was said, ‘your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac’; concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead. By faith, Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even concerning things to come. By faith, Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff. By faith, Joseph, when his end was near, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel; and gave instructions concerning his bones.

echoes.text: Don't let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For your offspring will be named through Isaac.
echoes.note: The one formal quotation in the chapter (v. 18). That the promise runs ‘through Isaac’ is what makes the command to sacrifice Isaac the supreme test — and the ground for the inference that God ‘is able to raise up even from the dead.’ The surrounding narrative (the tents, the binding, Jacob worshiping on his staff at Gen 47:31 LXX) is woven in as allusion.

echoes.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father's house, and go to the land that I will show you.”
echoes.note: ‘Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out… not knowing where he went’ (v. 8) retells the call of Gen 12:1–4. High verbal volume in the verbs of going out and obeying; the founding act of faith for the whole roll-call.

echoes.text: They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood.
echoes.note: ‘Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac’ (v. 17) retells the Aqedah (Gen 22, here v. 9, the binding). The narrative is reused whole and read past itself — the near-sacrifice becomes a figure of resurrection: ‘figuratively speaking, he received him back from the dead.’

echoes.text: God said, “No, but Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son. You shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.”
echoes.note: ‘Sarah herself received power to conceive… past age’ (v. 11) alludes to the promise of Gen 17:19 and its fulfillment at 21:1–2. The thematic point — the impossibility of the birth — is exactly what ‘counted him faithful who had promised’ requires.

echoes.text: Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
echoes.note: The fulfillment paired with the promise of 17:19: Sarah bore Isaac ‘when she was past age.’ Low verbal volume, but high coherence — the late-life birth is the very ground of the ‘as good as dead… stars and sand’ paradox in v. 12.

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your offspring be.”
echoes.note: ‘As many as the stars of the sky’ (v. 12) lifts the star-promise of Gen 15:5. Recurrence is decisive: the paired ‘stars… and sand’ formula returns from Gen 22:17, and the same image already anchored 6:13–14 — the most-repeated promise to Abraham.

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your offspring will possess the gate of his enemies.
echoes.note: ‘As innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore’ (v. 12) completes the doubled ‘stars and sand’ formula of Gen 22:17 — the oath sworn at the binding. Already quoted at Heb 6:13–14, so the recurrence test is satisfied across the letter.

echoes.text: I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.
echoes.note: ‘Strangers and pilgrims on the earth… dwelling in tents’ (vv. 9, 13) echoes Abraham's self-description at Gen 23:4, ‘a stranger and a foreigner.’ The pilgrim motif is the interpretive hinge — the patriarchs ‘desire a better country, a heavenly one.’

echoes.text: He came near, and kissed him. He smelled the smell of his clothing, and blessed him, and said, “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which Yahweh has blessed.”
echoes.note: ‘Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau… concerning things to come’ (v. 20) alludes to the deathbed blessing of Gen 27. Low volume, but the explicit naming of Isaac, Jacob, and Esau pins the source; faith is read as confidence in ‘things to come.’

echoes.text: He said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Israel bowed himself on the bed's head.
echoes.note: ‘Jacob… worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff’ (v. 21) follows the Greek of Gen 47:31, which reads ‘staff’ (matteh) where the Hebrew has ‘bed’ (mittah) — the same unpointed consonants. Availability again (Hays): the author's Septuagint gave him the staff. The blessing of Joseph's sons (Gen 48) is alluded to in the same breath.

echoes.text: He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day,”
echoes.note: ‘Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph’ (v. 21) retells Gen 48, where the dying patriarch blesses Ephraim and Manasseh. Reused as narrative rather than cited; coheres with the chapter's deathbed-faith pattern (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph all blessing what they will not see).

echoes.text: Joseph took an oath from the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
echoes.note: ‘Joseph… made mention of the departure of the children of Israel; and gave instructions concerning his bones’ (v. 22) closely retells Gen 50:24–25. High verbal volume — ‘departure’ and ‘bones’ both echo the oath; faith as confidence in an exodus Joseph would never see.

pericopes.text: By faith, Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were not afraid of the king's commandment. By faith, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to share ill treatment with God's people, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time; accounting the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward. By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible. By faith, he kept the Passover, and the sprinkling of the blood, that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them. By faith, they passed through the Red Sea as on dry land. When the Egyptians tried to do so, they were swallowed up. By faith, the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith, Rahab the prostitute, didn't perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace.

echoes.text: Moses and the Passover, the blood on the doorposts, the crossing of the Red Sea, the fall of Jericho, and Rahab's welcome of the spies (Exodus 12–14; Joshua 2; 6).
echoes.note: Faith demonstrated not by citation but by retelling — Moses, the Passover, the sea, Jericho, Rahab compressed into a litany of ‘by faith.’ Figural reuse of whole narratives: the Old Testament itself becomes the cloud of witnesses of 12:1.

echoes.text: The woman conceived, and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
echoes.note: ‘Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months… because they saw that he was a beautiful child’ (v. 23) is a near-verbatim retelling of Exod 2:2. High verbal volume — ‘hidden three months’ and the ‘fine/beautiful child’ both carry over.

echoes.text: In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers, and looked at their burdens. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his brothers.
echoes.note: ‘Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing… ill treatment with God's people’ (vv. 24–25) interprets Exod 2:11–15 — Moses casting his lot with the oppressed Hebrews. The narrative is reused and theologized (‘the reproach of Christ’).

echoes.text: The blood shall be to you for a token on the houses where you are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and there shall no plague be on you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: ‘He kept the Passover, and the sprinkling of the blood, that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them’ (v. 28) retells Exod 12 — the blood-token that turns the destroyer aside. High thematic coherence with the letter's blood-and-atonement argument.

echoes.text: The children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
echoes.note: ‘They passed through the Red Sea as on dry land… the Egyptians… were swallowed up’ (v. 29) retells Exod 14. The same deliverance/judgment doubling — dry ground for Israel, drowning for Egypt — is reused whole as an act of faith.

echoes.text: So the people shouted and the priests blew the trumpets. When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight in front of him, and they took the city.
echoes.note: ‘The walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days’ (v. 30) retells Josh 6. The ‘seven days’ detail carries directly from the narrative; the fall comes not by siege-works but by faith.

echoes.text: But Rahab the prostitute, her father's household, and all that she had, Joshua saved alive. She lives in the middle of Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers, whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
echoes.note: ‘Rahab the prostitute, didn't perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace’ (v. 31) retells Josh 2; 6:22–25. Rahab the outsider set among the faithful; her welcome of the spies is read as the faith that spared her.

pericopes.text: What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets; who, through faith subdued kingdoms, worked out righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, from weakness were made strong, grew mighty in war, and caused foreign armies to flee. Women received their dead by resurrection. Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others were tried by mocking and scourging, yes, moreover by bonds and imprisonment. They were stoned. They were sawn apart. They were tempted. They were slain with the sword. They went around in sheep skins and in goat skins; being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated (of whom the world was not worthy), wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth. These all, having had testimony given to them through their faith, didn't receive the promise, God having provided some better thing concerning us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

echoes.text: Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah (Judges); David and Samuel (1–2 Samuel); ‘stopped the mouths of lions’ and ‘quenched fire’ (Daniel 6; 3); and the tortured who looked for ‘a better resurrection’ (2 Maccabees 6–7).
echoes.note: The roll-call accelerates into a blur of unnamed sufferers. The tortured who refused release ‘that they might obtain a better resurrection’ allude to the Maccabean martyrs (2 Macc 7) — Scripture and the example of the faithful read together as one witness. The figural method at full speed.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Gideon, “By the three hundred men who lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into your hand.”
echoes.note: ‘Gideon… subdued kingdoms… caused foreign armies to flee’ (vv. 32–34) names the judge whose three hundred routed Midian (Judg 6–8). A representative verse for the Judges cluster (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah); the deliverers are reused as exemplars of faith, not cited.

echoes.text: My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions' mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.
echoes.note: ‘Stopped the mouths of lions’ (v. 33) is a near-verbatim allusion to Dan 6:22, where the angel ‘shut the lions' mouths.’ High verbal volume on the distinctive image — among the clearest links in the unnamed list.

echoes.text: The satraps, the deputies, and the governors, and the king's counselors, being gathered together, saw these men, that the fire had no power on their bodies.
echoes.note: ‘Quenched the power of fire’ (v. 34) alludes to Dan 3:27 — the three in the furnace on whom ‘the fire had no power.’ Paired with the lions of Dan 6 in the same line, the two Daniel deliverances stand side by side.

echoes.text: So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine, and killed him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.
echoes.note: ‘David’ (v. 32), who ‘grew mighty in war’ and ‘caused foreign armies to flee,’ is represented by the defeat of Goliath. Low volume (a name, not a phrase), but David and Samuel are explicitly named, anchoring the Samuel-narratives in the litany.

echoes.text: Yahweh listened to the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
echoes.note: ‘Women received their dead by resurrection’ (v. 35) alludes to the widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24). The plural ‘women’ pairs it with the Shunammite of 2 Kings 4 — two raised sons, one phrase.

echoes.text: Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself out on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
echoes.note: The second ‘woman’ who ‘received her dead’ (v. 35) is the Shunammite, whose son Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:32–37). Together with 1 Kings 17 it justifies the plural and sets up the contrast with those who chose death for ‘a better resurrection.’

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: ‘Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection’ (v. 35) draws on the Maccabean mother and seven sons (2 Macc 7), who refused release in hope of resurrection. The verbal link is ‘resurrection’/‘raise up… to renewal of life’ — a Second Temple, non-canonical witness read alongside Scripture.

echoes.text: But he, welcoming death with renown rather than life with pollution, advanced of his own accord to the instrument of torture, but first spat forth the flesh,
echoes.note: ‘Others were tortured… tried by mocking and scourging’ (vv. 35–36) also recalls the aged Eleazar of 2 Macc 6:18–31, who ‘advanced of his own accord to the instrument of torture.’ Contested and faint — a deuterocanonical example of voluntary martyrdom folded into the litany of the persecuted faithful.

echoes.text: [pseudepigraphal — not in WEB] The Ascension/Martyrdom of Isaiah recounts that Isaiah was sawn in two with a wood-saw at the order of King Manasseh (Mart. Isa. 5:1–14).
echoes.note: ‘They were sawn apart’ (v. 37) has no canonical referent; the early Jewish-Christian tradition that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh (Martyrdom of Isaiah, alluded to by Justin and the rabbis) is the standard identification. Pseudepigraphal and faint, but the otherwise-unexplained verb ‘sawn’ tips the balance (Hays' availability/satisfaction).

pericopes.text: Therefore let us also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don't grow weary, fainting in your souls. You have not yet resisted to blood, striving against sin;

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God’ (v. 2) sounds Ps 110:1 a final time — the verse first echoed at 1:3 and quoted at 1:13 now crowns the runner who finished the race.

pericopes.text: and you have forgotten the exhortation which reasons with you as with children, ‘My son, don't take lightly the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are reproved by him; For whom the Lord loves, he chastens, and scourges every son whom he receives.’ It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn't discipline? But if you are without discipline, of which all have been made partakers, then are you illegitimate, and not children. Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Shall we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits, and live? For they indeed, for a few days, punished us as seemed good to them; but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness. All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised thereby. Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed.

echoes.text: My son, don’t despise Yahweh’s discipline, neither be weary of his reproof: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
echoes.note: Wisdom's word on a father's discipline, applied to suffering: hardship is not God's absence but his fathering. The closing exhortation then borrows Isaiah's ‘strengthen the weak hands and feeble knees’ (Isa 35:3) and Proverbs' ‘make level paths’ (Prov 4:26).
echoes.lxxText: My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loves, he rebukes, and scourges every son whom he receives.

echoes.text: You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.
echoes.note: ‘What son is there whom his father doesn't discipline?’ (v. 7) restates the father-son discipline axiom of Deut 8:5 — the wilderness theology that hardship is paternal training, not abandonment. Strong thematic coherence (Hays) reinforcing the quoted Prov 3:11–12; the disciplining ‘father’ language is shared verbatim in sense. LXX and Hebrew agree here (‘as a man chastens his son’).

echoes.text: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.
echoes.note: ‘Lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees’ (v. 12) lifts Isaiah's oracle of comfort to the discouraged almost word for word — high verbal volume on the two paired body-parts. The LXX of Isa 35:3 (‘weak hands… feeble knees’) is the form Hebrews follows; the eschatological highway context (Isa 35) matches Hebrews' race imagery.

echoes.text: Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.
echoes.note: ‘Make straight paths for your feet’ (v. 13) echoes Prov 4:26 LXX (‘make straight/level tracks for your feet’) — Wisdom's image of the level, unswerving path, paired here with the lame foot to be healed. Verbal volume is high in the Greek; the LXX ‘straight tracks’ diverges from the Hebrew ‘ponder the path.’

echoes.text: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.
echoes.note: ‘The peaceful fruit of righteousness’ (v. 11) faintly recalls the wisdom idiom ‘fruit of the righteous’ (Prov 11:30). Low volume — a stock metaphor rather than a pointed citation; offered for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.
echoes.note: The collocation ‘peaceful fruit of righteousness’ (v. 11) may also draw on Isa 32:17, where righteousness yields ‘peace’ and quietness. Contested and faint — the link rests on the shared righteousness/peace pairing, not distinctive wording.

pericopes.text: Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord, looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it; lest there be any sexually immoral person, or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal. For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears.

echoes.text: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal, and later, rejected, sought the blessing with tears (Genesis 25:29–34; 27:30–40).
echoes.note: Esau the cautionary figure — the brother who traded an eternal inheritance for an appetite. ‘Root of bitterness’ also alludes to Deut 29:18 (a root ‘bearing poison’). The warning: do not be the one who despised the birthright.

echoes.text: When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with an exceeding great and bitter cry, and said to his father, ‘Bless me, even me also, my father.’ … Esau lifted up his voice, and wept. … ‘By your sword will you live, and you will serve your brother.’
echoes.note: ‘He was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears’ (v. 17) draws directly on the second Esau scene — the irreversible lost blessing and Esau's ‘exceeding great and bitter cry.’ High historical/verbal coherence: the ‘tears’ and the finality of the verdict come from Gen 27, distinct from the birthright sale of Gen 25.

echoes.text: lest there should be among you man, woman, family, or tribe whose heart turns away today from Yahweh our God, to go to serve the gods of those nations; lest there should be among you a root that produces bitter poison;
echoes.note: ‘Any root of bitterness springing up’ (v. 15) is near-verbatim with Deut 29:18 LXX (‘a root springing up in bitterness/gall’). High volume and recurrence within the apostasy-warning theme. The LXX reads ‘root springing up in gall and bitterness’ where the Hebrew has ‘root bearing poison/wormwood’ — Hebrews follows the Greek.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: ‘Follow after peace with all men’ (v. 14) echoes the psalm's ‘seek peace, and pursue it’ (Ps 34:14) — the same verb of pursuit. Medium volume; the imperative to chase after peace is distinctive enough to register, and Ps 34 is a favored source in early Christian paraenesis.

pericopes.text: For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched, and that burned with fire, and to blackness, darkness, storm, the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them, for they could not stand that which was commanded, ‘If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned’; and so fearful was the appearance that Moses said, ‘I am terrified and trembling.’ But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable multitudes of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect, to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel.

echoes.text: You shall set bounds to the people all around, saying, ‘Be careful that you don't go up onto the mountain, or touch its border. Whoever touches the mountain shall be surely put to death.’ No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot through; whether it is animal or man, he shall not live.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany — fire, darkness, trumpet, the forbidden mountain — set against Mount Zion. ‘If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned’ quotes Exod 19:12–13; ‘I am terrified and trembling’ (v. 21) echoes Moses at Deut 9:19; and the ‘blood that speaks better than Abel’ recalls Gen 4:10. Three texts braided into the two-mountain contrast.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. … All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire … When the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice.
echoes.note: The whole Sinai sensorium of v. 18–19 — fire, the burning mountain, the trumpet that grows louder, ‘the voice of words’ — is drawn from the theophany narrative of Exod 19:16–19. High verbal volume across multiple distinctive items (trumpet, fire, voice answering); this is the descriptive backbone behind the quoted prohibition.

echoes.text: You came near and stood under the mountain. The mountain burned with fire to the heart of the sky, with darkness, cloud, and thick darkness.
echoes.note: The triad ‘blackness, darkness, storm’ (v. 18) reproduces the LXX of Deut 4:11 (‘darkness, gloom, and storm/tempest’) almost verbatim — three nouns in sequence that the Hebrew renders differently. A textbook case of Hebrews following the Septuagint word-string; high volume on a rare cluster.

echoes.text: For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure with which Yahweh was angry against you to destroy you. But Yahweh listened to me that time also.
echoes.note: ‘Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling”’ (v. 21) ascribes to the Sinai scene Moses' confession of terror, which in Scripture stands at Deut 9:19 (the golden-calf aftermath: ‘I was afraid/terrified’). Medium volume — Hebrews telescopes the fear onto Sinai; the ‘I am terrified’ wording matches the LXX ekphobos.

echoes.text: All the people perceived the thunderings, the lightnings, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking. When the people saw it, they trembled, and stayed at a distance. They said to Moses, ‘Speak with us yourself, and we will listen; but don't let God speak with us, lest we die.’
echoes.note: ‘Those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them’ (v. 19) paraphrases the people's plea at Exod 20:18–19 — they ask that God speak no more lest they die. Solid thematic and historical coherence; medium because it is summary rather than citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.’
echoes.note: ‘The blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’ (v. 24) presupposes Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries out from the ground.’ High coherence: Hebrews contrasts the two crying bloods — Abel's for vengeance, Christ's for mercy. The personified, speaking blood is the distinctive shared element.

echoes.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the north sides, the city of the great King.
echoes.note: ‘You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God’ (v. 22) draws on the Zion-theology of Ps 48:1–2, where Mount Zion is ‘the city of the great King.’ The pairing of Mount Zion with ‘city of God’ is the distinctive collocation; high coherence with Hebrews' heavenly-Jerusalem motif.

echoes.text: ‘At that time Michael will stand up … and there will be a time of trouble … At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.’
echoes.note: ‘The assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) draws on the apocalyptic book-of-life motif, classically Dan 12:1 (‘everyone found written in the book’ is delivered). Medium volume; the enrollment/registration image is the link, shared with Exod 32:32.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.
echoes.note: ‘Enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) also recalls the heavenly book of Exod 32:32, the earliest ‘book which you have written.’ Lower volume than Dan 12:1; offered as the seed-text of the enrollment image for maximal coverage.
